#236. Giving Marjorie Taylor Greene a platform isn't good for America

Editor’s Note:  Dean Obeidallah, a former attorney, is the host of SiriusXM radio’s daily program “The Dean Obeidallah Show.” Follow him @DeanObeidallah@masto.ai. The opinions expressed in this commentary are his own. View more opinion on CNN.

Last year, GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia spoke at a white nationalist event organized by Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes that caused Republican leaders to denounce her.

Last week, Greene’s Twitter account was temporarily suspended by the Elon Musk-headed platform over a tweet with a graphic referring to a “Trans Day of Vengeance,” as she denounced a planned transgender rights rally.

And come Tuesday, Greene has announced plans to protest in New York City when former President Donald Trump is expected to be arraigned on an indictment of more than 30 counts, calling the proceedings against him an “unconstitutional WITCH HUNT!”

But on Sunday, Greene was featured on CBS’ “60 Minutes” in an interview the long-running show promoted on Twitter with the tease: “Republican Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, nicknamed MTG, isn’t afraid to share her opinions, no matter how intense and in-your-face they are. She sits down with Lesley Stahl this Sunday on 60 Minutes.” The images attached to this tweet by “60 Minutes” include Greene and Stahl walking through the US Capitol, taking a stroll outside and Greene showing Stahl something on her phone.

It's time for Marjorie Taylor Greene to go

In the segment that aired Sunday night, Stahl noted the congresswoman had moved from the fringe to the GOP’s front row in two years despite a “sharp tongue” and “some pretty radical views” as well as “over the top” comments such as “the Democrats are a party of pedophiles.” Stahl also referred to video of Greene chasing a Parkland, Florida, school shooting survivor, still maintaining that the 2020 election was stolen and failing to criticize Trump over spending. (The interview was conducted before news of his indictment.)

But Stahl didn’t mention Greene spoke at a white nationalist event a year ago while a member of Congress or her extreme anti-Muslim views and her defense of January 6 rioters.

Criticism of CBS for amplifying Greene has been swift and well-deserved even before the program aired. Former GOP Rep. Adam Kinzinger of Illinois tweeted beforehand: “Wow. Insane that 60 min would do this.” (Kinzinger is a CNN senior political commentator.)

Journalist Molly Jong-Fast also slammed “60 Minutes” with the tweet: “Attention is currency and 60 minutes is spending its currency on the Jewish space lasers woman.” (Jong-Fast was apparently referring to Greene’s past claim that a massive California wildfire was started by “a laser” beamed from space controlled by a prominent Jewish banking family.)

David Hogg, who survived the 2018 horrific school shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland and has since become an activist against gun violence, responded, “I look forward to your questions about why she thinks school shootings are fake and why she’s supported QAnon.”

Greene amplified the conspiracy theory — two years before being elected to Congress — that the Parkland shooting that took 17 lives was staged. And in 2019, Greene appeared on video confronting Hogg outside the Capitol when he was championing laws to save lives from gun violence, screaming that the then-teenager was a “coward.” She also called Hogg “#littleHitler” on social media.

Greene’s own tweet promoting Sunday’s segment was not filled with her typical smears of “fake news” when she doesn’t like the coverage. Rather, Greene urged people to tune in as she praised “60 Minutes” host Stahl (and misspelled her first name): “It was an honor to spend a few days with the legendary icon Leslie Stahl and talented crew @60Minutes.” Greene added, “Leslie is a trailblazer for women in journalism. And while we may disagree on some issues, I respect her greatly.”

Now, it is true that “60 Minutes” over its 50-plus-year history has featured what the show has dubbed “controversial” guests. These include a 2000 interview with Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, whose 1995 terrorist attack left 168 dead, including 19 children. And the show did a 1979 interview with Iran’s Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.

Perhaps “60 Minutes” views Greene — who has repeatedly downplayed and even defended the January 6, 2021, attack plus called for the GOP to become the party of “Christian nationalism” — in the vein of its long list of controversial guests. (CBS had not responded to a request from CNN for comment at time of publishing.)

However, the choice of Greene as a guest instantly recalls the comments of then-CBS CEO Les Moonves during Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign when he admitted that Trump’s candidacy “may not be good for America, but it’s damn good for CBS.” Moonves added, “The money’s rolling in and this is fun. … (T)his is going to be a very good year for us,” concluding, “Sorry. It’s a terrible thing to say. But bring it on, Donald. Keep going.”

Moonves may be gone from CBS, but it appears his mindset continues at “60 Minutes.” And that may be good for “60 Minutes,” but it’s definitely not good for America.

#235. Wi-Fi 8 is an attempt to fix the biggest problem with wireless internet

Because perfection currently remains just out of range.

Sometimes, better doesn't mean faster. With Wi-Fi 7 realistically capping out at about 23 Gbps (a number virtually nobody will see in the real world), speed is more than covered in the current generation. At this point, the biggest concern is reliability. Released in 2024, Wi-Fi 7 has been known to suffer from pain points like poor stability, weak wall penetration, and relatively short range.

Wi-Fi 8, which is still in development, is designed to address the considerable reliability issues plaguing the internet today. Final approval is expected in 2028, although companies like ASUS and TP-Link wasted no time announcing their first Wi-Fi 8 router based on the draft spec.

Most home internet plans offer speeds of a few hundred megabits per second, which older Wi-Fi 6 routers should handle with ease. For faster speeds, like a 2 Gbps fiber connection, Wi-Fi 7 can largely keep up (especially if you're sitting right next to the router). Wi-Fi 8 shifts the focus to stability, aiming to plug the holes that lead to shaky connections. It's being designed to fix common issues, like a weak signal in one part of the house, an apartment building with 20 networks competing for airtime or a clunky mesh handoff when walking between rooms.

The underlying standard, 802.11bn, is nicknamed "Ultra High Reliability," accentuating its focus on consistency and stability. Wi-Fi 8 should achieve 25 percent better throughput for weak signals, 25 percent fewer dropped packets (especially when moving between access points) and 25 percent lower latency at the shakiest moments.

The main way it gets there relates to how access points work together. Today's routers share channels by taking turns, and not always in the most efficient manner. Wi-Fi 8 refines that by letting compatible access points coordinate when each one transmits. That will make the most sense with mesh systems.

Although you can buy an ASUS gaming router or mesh system built on Wi-Fi 8 today, with a TP-Link model coming soon in some regions, they won't make much difference yet. For the upgrades to show themselves, both the router and the device (phone, laptop or tablet) on the other end need to support it as well.

So buying one now is more about investing in the future than some mythical immediate payoff. (Not that you'd know it from the marketing.) And since these first devices are built on a draft spec, there's no guarantee they'll support everything in the final version.

Eventually, Wi-Fi 8 should be worthwhile, especially if you live in a congested building or use a mesh network. Just be prepared to wait a year or two before you reap the benefits. For now, Wi-Fi 7 is still a perfectly reasonable choice for a new router. And if yours isn't positioned ideally, moving it to a central location will likely do more than any new standard, whether draft or final, will

#233. How to get the most protection from your Ring camera security system

Simply putting the camera on your front door may not be enough.

If you are going to use Ring, it's vital to maximize your setup's efficiency. Some of the company's products can be costly, and your goal here is to deter and record intruders (although you'll need a Ring subscription to do this), not just maintain an illusion of security. If that's all you care about, you might as well slap a few ADT stickers on your home along with a "Beware of Dog" sign.

Efficiency isn't about covering the widest area — it's about thinking like a thief, yet spending as little as possible for the results you need. You also need to be concerned about minimizing false alerts.

Your first consideration should be capturing all possible points of entry — and we mean all of them. Don't just position cameras over your doorways. If you've got a side alley, for example, it's possible that an intruder could climb a fence and break in without ever appearing on your door-based video feeds. Give your outdoor cameras overlapping views when possible, and make sure they're installed around 9 feet high, excluding doorbells. This will not only ensure a wide field of view, but make it harder for intruders to smash or tamper with your equipment. That said, cameras should also be easily visible beyond your property. Any halfway intelligent thief is going to think twice if they know they're being recorded.

Ring is eager to sell you indoor cameras, but these aren't actually necessary unless you're hoping to monitor a child, pet or guests. By the time an intruder makes it indoors, all you're really doing is capturing further evidence of their crimes. If you do buy indoor cameras, position them high in the corners for broad coverage, with an eye toward entryways.

Once cameras are in position, be sure to spend time customizing their Motion Zones via the Ring app. This can prevent unwanted motion detection from objects such as passing traffic or trees blowing in the wind. But really, you'll also want to turn on Advanced Motion Detection if a camera supports it, and most importantly, Smart Alerts. These let you narrow alerts to people, packages and/or vehicles, so when you receive notifications on your phone, you'll know to take them seriously instead of tuning them out. Smart Alerts do require a subscription, so remember that before you come to depend on them.

A factor that's all too easy to neglect is redundancy. You should always have a backup battery available for your cameras powered by removable batteries, for example, because it can take hours to fully recharge one. You may also want spare cables or installation tools.

Even more critical is the quality of your Wi-Fi network, since you need a stable signal for uninterrupted video. Be sure to test for any weak spots or dead zones, and consider upgrading to a mesh system if you can't fix them with better router placement. You don't need to go with Amazon's eero routers, but if you can't afford any downtime whatsoever, look into models with cellular backup features. These can keep your entire network online at the cost of a monthly fee. You may want power backup too, however, and that can get very expensive on the whole-home level.

Lastly, don't forget to consider supplementing your cameras with door and window sensors (tied to a Ring Alarm system), as well as automatic lighting. While newer Ring cameras do have great night vision, lights from Ring or otherwise can improve video clarity further and make intruders visible to everyone. Just make sure lights aren't blaring into your neighbor's windows or too easily triggered by people passing by.

#232. James Webb telescope finds ice older than the star it orbits

Radiation and collisions reshape the planetary building materials.

Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice.

The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars.

Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It’s what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets.

The outer parts of the disk are far enough from the star that water and other volatile molecules should freeze into solid ice. The disk holds a large reservoir of carbon monoxide gas, which ultraviolet light from the star should destroy within 50 to 300 years. For that gas to still be there, something must keep replenishing it—most likely it’s released from ice when volatile-rich comets collide. The properties of the planet Beta Pictoris b also suggest it formed from ice-rich material.

Yet despite plenty of reasons to suspect the system is full of ice, earlier searches have failed to find it. Attempts to detect water vapor found nothing, and a search for the telltale dip that water ice leaves in starlight at a wavelength of 3 micrometers also failed.

According to theoretical models, ultraviolet radiation from the star can destroy small grains of pure ice faster than collisions can produce them. On the other hand, grains of dirty ice, mixed with other molecules, should survive longer.

Betti and her colleagues observed Beta Pictoris on December 7, 2023, using Webb’s Near Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec). They operated it in a mode that records a full spectrum, from 0.6 to 5.2 micrometers, for every point in the image. After subtracting the overwhelming glare of the star, the team measured how much starlight the disk’s dust reflects at each wavelength to look for the fingerprints of ices.

Water ice absorbs light strongly near 3 micrometers, while carbon dioxide ice absorbs either at 4.27 micrometers or 4.39 micrometers when it contains the heavier carbon-13 isotope. The team first mapped the water ice features across the disk and found they were strikingly uniform. They then extracted detailed spectra from two spots on opposite sides of the star, each roughly 100 astronomical units out.

Both spectra showed water and carbon dioxide ices, the latter in both its common form and the rarer carbon-13 version. But the shape of those features turned out to tell us more than the fact they were there.

The carbon dioxide features were shifted slightly toward shorter wavelengths and were much broader than those of pure carbon dioxide ice measured in the lab. The team says in the paper that this is how carbon dioxide behaves when its molecules are trapped inside water ice. In other words, the two ices aren’t sitting side by side as separate grains—they are thoroughly mixed, which makes it the kind of dirty ice that models suggested could survive the star’s ultraviolet radiation.

The team calculated that there is slightly more than one carbon dioxide molecule for every 10 water molecules, meaning it’s about 11 percent of the ice. That falls within the 2.5 to 30 percent range measured in Solar System comets and the 7 to 20 percent seen in the ice of disks around other newborn stars. It means the ices of Beta Pictoris may have formed through the same processes as in our own Solar System, building up on dust grains in cold, dense, water-rich clouds during the earliest stages of star formation.

The structure of the water ice also pointed in this direction. When water freezes at moderate temperatures, its molecules settle into an orderly crystal lattice, and crystalline ice produces a sharp peak in the spectrum just above 3 micrometers. That peak was absent at Beta Pictoris. The ice is almost entirely amorphous, a disordered, glass-like solid that forms when water molecules freeze so fast and so cold that they stick wherever they land. The team estimates that less than 7 percent of the water ice in the system is crystalline, which is somewhat surprising.

Models predicted that ice in debris disks should mostly be crystalline. For amorphous ice to stay in that form, it has to remain colder than about 100 Kelvin, or minus 173° Celsius. Otherwise, something has to keep breaking up its crystal structure, such as high-energy ultraviolet light, cosmic rays, or particles streaming from the star. Either way, the researchers concluded the ice most likely formed in the interstellar medium, long before the planets of Beta Pictoris began to take shape.

The remaining question was how the icy grains got spread so evenly across the disk.

The team argues that this even ice distribution requires frequent collisions among planetesimals. Each collision would release fresh icy dust, including ice that had been buried and protected deep inside the colliding bodies, replenishing what the starlight destroys. We already have evidence that such collisions do happen. Earlier infrared images revealed a curved, lopsided streak of dust in the southwestern arm of the disk, thought to be debris from a violent collision a little less than halfway out from the star.

Betti’s team’s findings support the idea that the disk’s carbon monoxide gas comes from colliding icy bodies and offer an explanation of how ice can survive in an environment constantly exposed to ultraviolet light. What the team could not do is determine exactly how much crystalline ice is present or rule out other molecules hiding in the mixture.

But if a young planetary system 64 light-years away may have started with much the same icy ingredients as ours, then primordial, interstellar ice might be a common ingredient of planetary systems in general. This means the raw materials for water-rich, potentially habitable worlds might be common, too.

Science, 2026. DOI: 10.1126/science.adw7770

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#231. Asian love ballads test Eurovision’s winning song formula.

Carmelle of the Philippines defeated 10 competitors at the first edition of the high-camp event in Asia, held in Bangkok.

The Eurovision Song Contest crowned its first Asia champion in Bangkok on Saturday, in an event that tested whether a high-camp singing competition with an ardent fan base could appeal to audiences in a new market.

Carmelle of the Philippines was declared the winner of the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia, beating out artists and original songs from 10 other countries: Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Mongolia, Nepal, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam. The show was live-streamed on YouTube and broadcast by television stations across the region.

Eurovision has been a fixture of the European cultural calendar since it began in 1956. Past winners include Sweden’s ABBA and the Canadian chanteuse Celine Dion, who represented Switzerland in 1988.

Asian artists have readily embraced the kitschy outfits and spectacular sets that are part of Eurovision tradition, with costumes that include traditional dress, as well as feathered capes and sequined corsets. Malaysia’s performer plans to enter the stage in a giant teardrop.

But the Eurovision format has not been tested in Asia. Fans and regional partners have expressed concern in recent weeks that budget constraints, production issues and weak audience demand could imperil the spinoff. Organizers say the contest could take time to build an audience.

“It would be profoundly arrogant to think that just because we have a heritage brand and a huge global audience for the European show, that we would walk in and demand it to be the same here,” said Martin Green, the European Broadcasting Union’s director of the Eurovision Song Contest. “Like any new thing, it needs to find its roots.”

Two previous attempts to take the competition to Asia were abandoned by the European Broadcasting Union, which owns Eurovision, and its partners in the region. A Eurovision spinoff in the United States, NBC’s American Song Contest, ran for one season in 2022.

The Asian edition kicking off on Saturday is far smaller than its European counterpart. Eurovision organizers said they were in talks with more countries to join future seasons. They include China, Japan and India, whose music industries have global reach.

“Bringing the world together through music is a fundamentally good idea,” Mr. Green said. “Europe shouldn’t keep it to itself.”

Ballads: Nine of the competition’s 11 participating countries picked performers singing about love in a wide range of styles, from ballads to a cappella hip-hop. Their choices suggest that the bombastic music often associated with victors of the European edition might not be a winning formula for Asian viewers. Read more ›

Fans: Our reporter spoke to some of the fans who traveled to Bangkok for Eurovision. Read more ›

Politics: Geopolitics have long intruded on the European edition of the Eurovision Song Contest, but they were not really a factor as the event prepared to expand into Asia. Read more ›

No shows: For a competition meant to introduce the diversity of Asian pop music to the world, the lineup for the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia has several notable absences, starting with China and India. Read more ›

As Thailand’s Mang and Daou waited to learn whether they had won, the 26-year-old Mang was shown onscreen crying as if she couldn’t take the tension. That’s the sort of emotion needed to make Eurovision’s expansion into Asia a success. Acts have to want the title. But the show will also need the big Asian nations -- India, Japan and China -- to buy in, and much could now depend on the reaction in the Philippines to Carmelle’s win. The event was far less spectacular than a typical Eurovision in Europe. It also featured far too many ballads for my taste, but it was a fun afternoon’s viewing.

Shiesam Flores, 27, a clerk from the eastern region of Bicol in the Philippines, has been watching the show at a party with her friends — and hoping that Carmelle would prevail.

“It was nerve-wracking, nail biting suspense!” she said. “But we know she would win! What a talent!”

The Philippines’ Carmelle wins the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, pushing Thailand’s Mang and Daou into second.

The crowd roared in disappointment as Malaysia got only 70 points from the public vote.

Thailand takes a massive lead thanks to the public vote, but the genius of this voting process is we won’t know whether the Philippines can overcome them until the last seconds.

The public gave Beatmosphere, from Bangladesh, just 19 points. They looked surprisingly happy after getting such a low total, and it’s now confirmed they’ve come in a distant last.

Dara has brought the Eurovision Asia trophy to the stage. It’s a sparkly gold microphone.

The public vote can be brutal, as some acts rapidly learn that few viewers liked them.

The jury votes are all in, and it’s close. The Philippines is first with 93 points, Vietnam second with 83 points and Malaysia third with 82 points. We’re about to learn how many points each country’s act received from the public, starting with the current last place act, Bangladesh’s beatboxing-heavy crew Beatmosphere. It has 16 points.

One of the best parts of Eurovision is how the public’s choice is often completely diffferent from those of the juries, so don’t worry if your favorite act isn’t top of the ranking after the jury votes are all in. The Philippine’s jury, the first we’ve heard from, just gave its 12 points to Malaysia. That doesn’t mean it’ll win

Fans are decked out in flags and sequins for the first-ever Asia Eurovision here in Bangkok.

The problem Eurovision has with interval acts like Jeff Satur is that their stagecraft, singing ability and melodies are often a million times better than the artists in competition. Satur, who has 1.4 million monthly listeners on Spotify and over five million Instagram fans, has dozens of camp dancers onstage and a statue of a dragon. He would have cruised to victory if he’d been in competition, especially because of his ability to hold high notes close to the range only dogs can hear.

Simon Robinson, one of the fans who traveled to Bangkok for the Eurovision Song Contest on Saturday, said that his history with the competition is nearly as long as its seven-decade run.

He was eight years old when he first watched it with his family in Yorkshire, England, when Britain's Mary Hopkin finished in second place behind Ireland’s Dana.

“I really liked the concept of bringing Europe together after the war,” said Mr. Robinson, 63, who now lives in Melbourne, Australia. He described the contest’s annual broadcast as a social activity for his family and neighbors.

“Eurovision helped to create the European identity,” he added.

Other fans had their own motivations for traveling to see the contest’s first Asian edition.

Some are Europeans living in Asia, on the hunt for nostalgia, while others are Americans who were eager to experience their first Eurovision.

Lee Hudson, an American television executive based in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, said that he gets emotional when he talks about Eurovision, which he has watched since 2012.

“The only reason I know any music from European countries is because I heard them on Eurovision,” he said. “Eurovision Asia makes sense because the musical cultures are distinct.”

Mr. Hudson said he still listens to Loreen’s “Euphoria,” which won the competition for Sweden in 2012.

It was also the first Eurovision that Drew Andrea watched from his home in Sydney. A year later, he got a passport to fly to Sweden for the 2013 edition, and has attended every final since. Coming to Bangkok for Eurovision Asia was much more affordable, he said.

“Asia understands the brief — the kitschy costumes, the dance music,” he said.

His top picks among the Asian performers were the Philippines’ Carmelle and Vietnam’s Toc Tien. “I think they hit the nail on the head with the song, staging, costume and traditional elements,” he said.

Luca Cian, a professor of marketing at the University of Virginia who grew up in Italy, said that Eurovision built a global fan base by offering a shared cultural experience.

“Millions of people across Europe watch it at the same moment,” he said. “Families have watch parties with food and drinks. There are public discussions. Rituals create community.”

Carmen Chung, a British accountant, said she hijacked her family’s holiday in Bangkok to attend Eurovision Asia with her brother Garry Chung, a banker who lives in Hong Kong. “We were raised on Eurovision,” she said of their childhood in Yorkshire.

European acts, she said, tend to copy whatever style of music won the previous year. “This year, because there are no expectations, everyone has just done their own thing,” she said. She and her brother said they were rooting for Bangladesh’s Beatmosphere, a beatboxing group that will perform an a cappella love song.

Martin Green, the director of the Eurovision Song Contest, said that about half of the tickets for Saturday’s final were purchased by “super fans” from outside Asia. Organizers have kept the inaugural show modest, with 11 participating countries and a 5,000-seat venue.

Mr. Andrea said he didn’t mind the small scale.

“I’m O.K. with humble beginnings as long as it keeps growing every year,” he said.

The Thai pop star Jeff Satur, a guest performer, got the high-camp memo.

The presenters are talking to the artists in the green room and trying to get them to talk excitedly about Bulgaria, the country that will host the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest. The winner tonight might get to perform at that event. That seems to be making this show less about Asia itself than a spin-off of the main Eurovision event

Eurovision voting involves two parts. Juries representing music industry professionals from each country are allocated half the votes, and the viewing public decides the other half. To try to build tension, the show always announces the jury votes first by going live to representatives from each country who reveals their top acts. In the European edition of the contest, some of those spokespeople are celebrities, and often they try to give mini speeches or make jokes. This part of the show is always awful. You have been warned.

There are a lot of European expatriates in this crowd. That much is obvious when Bulgaria’s Dara, the winner of this year’s Eurovision, takes the stage with her winning song, “Bangaranga.” Some fans even danced along with her choreography!

Mohamad Iqbal Dzulqarnain, an Aina Abdul fan in Kuala Lumpur, said he felt her performance was better than the recording version.

“She left no crumbs,” he said. “She is going to win the contest.”

For a competition meant to introduce the diversity of Asian pop music to the world, the lineup for the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia on Saturday had several notable absences.

For starters, the continent’s four most populous nations — China, India, Pakistan and Indonesia — were not there. Even Japan, a country globally considered a cultural powerhouse, was absent.

That left some of the region’s best-known musical cultures out of the mix. India has Bollywood hits. China has produced both Mandopop and Cantopop, the genre associated with Hong Kong pop stars. JPop was once huge across Asia.

As a result, the only large pop powerhouse in this contest was South Korea.

China’s absence is relatively simple to explain. Performers are entered by local broadcasters, and Eurovision has long had a messy relationship with China’s, which are heavily regulated and try to reflect the government’s social and political values. Mango TV once had a deal to broadcast the high-camp Eurovision to Chinese viewers, but Eurovision abruptly canceled it in 2018 after Mango TV censored acts whose performances featured gay themes. It also blurred rainbow flags in the performance arena.

Frank-Dieter Freiling, a former Eurovision official, said in an interview that such censorship was against Eurovision’s values and that the show’s organizers had historically barred broadcasters from airing the competition with delays.

It’s less clear why broadcasters from India, Pakistan, Japan and Indonesia did not participate. Assaf Blecher, Eurovision Asia’s executive producer, said that conversations with Chinese, Japanese and Indian broadcasters had not concluded in time. But he insisted that they “are knocking on our door.”

Not participating saved those countries the potential embarrassment of being the regional power that comes in last.

Just look to Europe, where Britain and Germany often perform badly at Eurovision. In this year’s show, Britain’s Look Mum No Computer placed last, scoring only one point, while Germany finished third from last. Whenever that happens, political commentators give interviews suggesting that the results reflect those countries’ poor standing across Europe.

Here at the watch party in Kathmandu, Pratik’s relatives are happy with his performance.

“His voice was cracking during the selection round in Nepal,” said Sunita Rai, his sister-in-law. “Today’s performance was much more powerful.”

His relatives have been on social media all night, urging their friends who live overseas to vote for him. (You can’t vote for your own country’s performer.)

The presenters have just announced a technical issue! When Laos’s Thinla performed earlier, she had an earpiece problem and was unable to hear her own music. So that explains why she sang so out of tune. They’re now playing a recording of an earlier performance to everyone to try to ensure the event is fair

Rizal Kamal, a senior adviser to the Arts, Live Festival and Events Association, an entertainment nonprofit based in Malaysia, said he felt that Aina Abdul was the right singer to represent the country at Eurovision.

“Aina is seasoned in major competitions and she knows how to wow both the judges and the audience,” he said. “I am filled with pride.”

Aina Abdul’s inventive wardrobe and her powerful voice sets her apart from the Asian peers, said Adriana Syuhaidah, a fan in Kuala Lumpur.

“She is the Lady Gaga of Malaysia,” she said.

When they sat down to plan the final show of the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest in Asia, the organizers faced a challenge: How could they introduce variety when most of the entries were slow-paced love songs?

Nine of the competition’s 11 participating countries picked performers singing about love in a wide range of styles, from ballads to a cappella hip-hop. Their choices suggest that the bombastic music often associated with victors of the European edition might not be a winning formula for Asian viewers.

“Europeans tend to prefer songs with a crescendo, a hook and a grand ending, but also a strong social message,” said Dean Vuletic, a historian of contemporary Europe at the University of Luxembourg who is an authority on Eurovision.

“The audience doesn’t want to see an innocuous pop song,” he said.

Electro-pop and dance songs have featured heavily on the list of Eurovision winners over the past decade. In May, Bulgaria’s Dara won with “Bangaranga,” a dance-pop song inspired by her diagnosis with attention deficit hyperactive disorder. Nemo, from Switzerland, won in 2024 with an EDM opera about their nonbinary identity, while in 2018, Israel’s Netta won with “Toy,” a pop anthem about female independence.

Some countries hold a nationwide contest to select an artist and a song to represent them in Eurovision, while others leave the choice to Eurovision’s local broadcasting partner. Audiences in the Philippines voted for Carmelle in a televised competition, for example, while Vietnam Television chose Toc Tien.

The two are considered front-runners in the Asian edition, with their high-energy folk-pop songs about female empowerment.

Malaysia’s Aina Abdul, another early favorite, will showcase her powerful vocals in “Bluest Sky,” a ballad with an orchestral arrangement that is about a troubled relationship. The track is reminiscent of “Wasted Love,” an opera-techno song that won Austria the European title in 2025.

Pratik Himal Rai of Nepal, who got married this summer, said love was easy to sing about because it can be understood across borders and languages.

“It is love that holds the world together,” he said in an interview.

He will sing “Ananta Maya” in Nepali. Other Eurovision Asia artists blend English lyrics with their national languages.

In Europe, every winning song after 2022 has been in English. That year’s champion, Ukraine's Kalush Orchestra, sang in their own language on “Stefania,” a hip-hop track that interspersed a Ukrainian lullaby with rap verses and traditional woodwind instruments.

Winning songs tend to blend a country’s national instruments and musical motifs with internationally trendy pop, Mr. Vuletic said.

A traditional Bhutanese flute can be heard in “Lhayi Semo,” Nyendra’s love ballad. Monetrey’s “I Let You Go” uses a Cambodian bamboo xylophone and a tro, a string instrument played with a bow. A kulintang, a percussion instrument made of eight brass gongs, keeps the fast beat in Carmelle’s “Sobra-Sobra.”

#230. What OPEC's surprise oil cut means for gas prices

OPEC and its allies’ surprise move to slash oil production will soon be felt at US gas pumps.

The group known as OPEC+ announced Sunday it would cut oil production by more than 1.6 million barrels a day starting in May, running through the end of the year. The news sent both Brent crude futures, the global oil benchmark, and WTI, the US benchmark, up about 6% in trading Monday.

The production cut announcement also had an immediate impact on gasoline futures, which will be passed onto US drivers much more quickly than the spike in oil prices. RBOB, the most closely watched wholesale gasoline price, was up about 8 cents a gallon, or about 3%, in morning trading.

“I think OPEC is reawakening the inflation monster,” said Tom Kloza, global head of energy analysis for OPIS, which tracks gas prices for AAA. “The White House has to be shocked and major-time pissed. It certainly alters the calculus for a while.”

The national average for US gas prices stood at $3.51, on Monday, according to AAA. Kloza said he could see it getting up to $3.80 to $3.90 in relatively short order thanks to the move by OPEC.

“We’re not going to get back to $5 a gallon. I don’t think we’re even going as high as $4,” he said. But he said by the end of the summer US drivers could be back above year-earlier prices, especially if there is a hurricane or other storms affecting production along the Gulf Coast.

The average US regular gas price a year ago stood at $4.19 a gallon in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the disruption that caused to world’s energy markets. Prices eventually reached a record $5.02 a gallon on June 14, before starting a slow but steady decline over the course of more than three months during which the average price fell every day. The decline was partly driven by the release of oil from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and partly by concerns that there could be a US or global recession that reduced the demand for gasoline.

Oil prices surge after OPEC+ producers announce surprise cuts

Even at $3.51, US gas prices were just below the $3.53 average on Feb. 23, 2022, the day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Kloza said one thing keeping prices from getting anywhere near the record levels of 2022 is that the US plans additional releases from the SPR, and US oil production and refining capacity are both up. But a cut of 1 million barrels a day of oil by OPEC+ will not be easy to make up.

“They have ability to cut production and they seem motivated to do so,” he said.

#229. AO3 is back online but with limited features

The outage lasted two weeks but full functionality is expected to resume soon.

After two weeks in the dark, popular fan fiction website Archive of Our Own (AO3) is back online. However, Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the nonprofit organization that runs AO3, said that some features have been temporarily disabled as a compromise to bring the site back earlier than the four-week mark, according to an update post on the website. OTW said that features like icons and external work importing are currently disabled, while works can only be downloaded in HTML format. The organization clarified that these features will be restored and that no icons have been deleted.

AO3 was taken offline at the end of October due to "evidence of a security incident" that OTW said would result in two to four weeks of downtime. Now that the open-source fan fiction repository is back online, its users may still run into some issues, according to OTW. The organization said it implemented an "intentional measure to help manage traffic," so users may experience delays with the website loading but can refresh to continue trying.

As for the site's data, OTW said that none of it was deleted, adding that user "works, bookmarks, kudos, etc. are still safe." OTW also managed to pause AO3's draft deletion feature so that no drafts were deleted during the downtime. Users should log back in and check on their drafts, though, since the feature will turn back on starting November 29 so that drafts longer than 30 days old will be deleted.

It's still unclear what the cause was, but OTW confirmed it was a "security incident" and that it would "not be sharing specifics about what mitigating changes are being made at this time." OTW added that it partnered with a security firm to review the incident and analyze the site to prevent future incidents. The update post said that OTW has "no reason to believe that the user database was compromised, though we cannot rule out that possibility," recommending that users change passwords, update linked emails and change passwords of any other sites that share a password with AO3 accounts.

#228. How to tell whether your car supports Apple CarPlay

Most newer cars do, but there are a few exceptions.

Apple CarPlay is one of the most useful pieces of in-car software out there, unifying navigation with the other iPhone features you might want to use while driving, like a music player. It's good enough that it can be a selling point to help you decide between two cars when you're looking to buy one. Fortunately, it's extremely easy to tell whether your car supports Apple CarPlay, and there are a few options for integrating it even without built-in support.

Apple maintains a list of every car model that currently supports CarPlay online. The list is extensive, covering basically every new car model from major manufacturers. A few notable exceptions are Tesla and Rivian, which don't support CarPlay at all. GM previously attempted to pull away from supporting Apple's software on newer models in favor of its own version but has since added CarPlay back.

There are also a few ways to check in person if a particular car you're looking at supports wireless CarPlay. With Bluetooth and Wi-Fi on your iPhone turned on, also set the car's dashboard to Bluetooth or wireless. Press the voice command button on the car's steering wheel, then see if the car appears on the list of available devices in Settings > General > CarPlay on your iPhone.

If you can connect your phone to the car's USB port, you'll get a prompt to activate wired CarPlay if the car supports it. You can also check the dashboard screen for a CarPlay option or look for a CarPlay symbol on the USB port, though even supported cars may not have the symbol in every case.

If you find yourself with a car that doesn't have integrated CarPlay support, there are a few ways you can add it yourself, though not without some hassle and expense. The easier method is to buy a third-party CarPlay screen to add to your car. Made by a variety of manufacturers, these screens can be mounted to your dashboard, essentially replacing your car's existing screen or adding one if you don't have one already. Most brands can interface with both CarPlay and Android Auto, letting you use all the software's functions on any vehicle. They're fairly inexpensive, typically around $100 or less, and can be moved from car to car. The downside is that you'll be relying on an extra piece of third-party hardware, and finding a good place to mount it can be tricky depending on your vehicle.

A permanent but more complicated solution is to install a CarPlay-compatible head unit. This will replace the car's stereo receiver (and screen if your car already has one) with a new screen capable of using Apple CarPlay. This option will likely be more expensive than just buying a screen, though some units can still be found in the $100 range. You'll also have to go through a more complex installation process or pay someone to do it for you, but the advantage is having an integrated unit rather than an extra peripheral to wrangle.

#227. Scientists film deepest ever fish on seabed off Japan

Sign up for CNN’s Wonder Theory science newsletter. Explore the universe with news on fascinating discoveries, scientific advancements and more.

Cruising at a depth of 8,336 meters (over 27,000 feet) just above the seabed, a young snailfish has become the deepest fish ever filmed by scientists during a probe into the abyss of the northern Pacific Ocean.

Scientists from University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology released footage of the snailfish on Sunday filmed last September by sea robots in deep trenches off Japan.

Along with the filming the deepest snailfish, the scientists physically caught two other specimens at 8,022 meters and set another record for the deepest catch.

Previously, the deepest snailfish ever spotted was at 7,703 meters in 2008, while scientists had never been able to collect fish from anywhere below 8,000 meters.

“What is significant is that it shows how far a particular type of fish will descend in the ocean,” said marine biologist Alan Jamieson, founder of the Minderoo-UWA Deep Sea Research Centre, who led the expedition.

Scientists are filming in the trenches off Japan as part of a 10-year study into the deepest fish populations in the world. Snailfish are members of Liparidae family, and while most snailfish live in shallow water, others survive at some of the greatest depths ever recorded, Jamieson said.

During the two-month survey last year, three “landers” – automatic sea robots fitted with high-resolution cameras – were dropped into three trenches – the Japan, Izu-Ogasawara and Ryukyu trenches – at varying depths.

In the Izu-Ogasawara trench, footage showed the deepest snailfish hovering calmly alongside other crustaceans on the seabed.

Jamieson classified the fish as a juvenile and said younger deep sea snailfish often stay as deep as possible to avoid being eaten by bigger predators that swim at shallower depths.

Another clip shot at between 7,500 and 8,200 meters in the same trench showed a colony of fish and crustaceans munching at bait tied to an undersea robot.

Images of the two captured snailfish – identified as Pseudoliparis belyaevi – provide a rare glimpse of the unique features that help the deep sea species survive the extreme environment.

They have tiny eyes, a translucent body, and their lack of swim bladder, which helps other fish float, works to their advantage, Jamieson said.

The professor said the Pacific Ocean is particularly conducive to vibrant activity due to its warm southern current, which encourages sea creatures to go deeper, while its abundant marine life provides a good source of food for bottom feeders.

Scientists would like to know more about creatures living at extreme depths, but cost is the constraint, Jamieson said, adding that each lander alone costs them $200,000 to assemble and operate.

“The challenges are that technology has been expensive and scientists don’t have a lot of money,” he said.

#226. SpaceX returned its Starship rocket on Saturday—but there's a catch

STARBASE, Texas—The black and silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position.

Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about one foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms.

Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket.

This was a breathtaking feat; a brilliant technical achievement that required the best engineering minds to think through a million different, difficult problems. And on Saturday evening, following a handful of practice runs into the Indian Ocean, they did it before the entire world.

Watching Starship launch from here a little less than a day earlier, and knowing it had orbited the planet multiple times, added to the sense of unreality in seeing this spaceship return to Earth under its own power, and be captured by the tower.

It felt like stepping into the future. SpaceX has dazzled us before, by landing rockets on barges and returning humans to space with Crew Dragon. But this flight took things to another level. Starships are huge. They carry a huge amount of energy coming back from orbit. And until a few years ago, it seemed beyond fantastical to think about capturing a rocket with what are essentially outsized chopsticks.

Humans have built reusable spacecraft that flew into orbit before. In the 1970s, flush with confidence after the triumphant Moon landings, NASA designed and built several Space Shuttles. They had solid rocket boosters that were fished from the ocean and reused. The large orange external tank was not recovered after each flight, but the orbiters went to space for two weeks, or even longer, before returning to Earth and landing on a runway.

The shuttles were engineering marvels. But during the return to Earth they acted as gliders, not igniting their engines. And their heat shields were delicate flowers, requiring painstaking refurbishment after each flight. At the outset of the shuttle program, the space agency contemplated sending dozens of humans into space at a time, and carrying cargo at a cost as low of $25 per pound.

Reality never matched these rosy projections. The crew space capped out at seven astronauts, and the cost-per-pound was closer to $25,000. Each orbiter cost an extraordinary amount of money to build; NASA only ever built five that went to space.

SpaceX has five Starships in an advanced state of development at Starbase today; and its factory houses the components for a dozen more. The company can currently manufacture a Starship upper stage in its South Texas Starfactory every three weeks. The factory was sized to produce a ship every three days. When SpaceX founder Elon Musk discussed these build targets in an interview five years ago, he sounded mad. But he no longer does.

The Space Shuttle was nearly a fully reusable space launch system, but it fell far short of low-cost, rapid launch. Over 30 years the vehicle made 135 flights. Within a few years SpaceX aims to fly 135 times a year, then thousands of times.

Such was the significance of Saturday. SpaceX aspires to fundamentally change the relationship between humanity and the heavens. The first step is to get the entire rocket back. SpaceX has now returned both elements of a Starship rocket safely to its launch tower. It will take time to reach a high rate of success with such landings, but Saturday’s safe return offered a proof of concept.

The landings will come with increasing frequency; and so will the launches. Over time SpaceX will perfect the heat shield that is likely to be the most difficult aspect of rapid reuse. And eventually, as difficult as it may be to believe, what we experienced with amazement this weekend will become routine. One day, we will take this all for granted.

#224. How to get warnings about speed cameras in Apple CarPlay

CarPlay is just the messenger, while your navigation app does all the hard work.

With all the rage and controversy over Flock cameras, speed cameras (or speed traps) have taken a back seat. Most of us have to deal with speed cameras (though they're banned in some states and limited in others), and Apple CarPlay is one way to handle them. While CarPlay itself doesn't send out speed camera warnings, alerts can be turned on for whichever navigation app you use. It stands to reason that Apple CarPlay users default to Apple Maps, but there are other, equally useful alternatives like Waze and Google Maps. There's always a caveat, however. Regardless of the nav app you use, mobile speed traps, by definition, move around a lot. Unless someone reports the new position on a given app, you won't get a warning.

Mobile speed detectors (in some form or another) have been around since the first speeding arrest in the US in 1899. A NYC taxicab driver named Jacob German was caught going 12 mph in an Electrobat (nearly the speed of light back then) in an 8 mph zone. The mobile units in those days were police officers on bicycles. Fortunately, modern technology provides drivers with information as it changes, but there's no such thing as a navigation app that knows where every camera is at all times.

In Apple Maps, there is no camera switch to toggle on or off. Camera alerts are automatic in supported regions. Waze, a compatible CarPlay navigation app, turns camera alerts on by default. You have the option to fine-tune them as well. In the Waze app, open Settings > Alerts and Reports > Reports > Cameras. Each camera type has its own toggles for "Show on map" and "Alert while driving." Make sure any changes made in the Waze app take place before connecting to CarPlay, because Waze only applies them the next time you connect and go for a drive.

Google Maps is similar yet has slightly different settings. On CarPlay, tap "Report" to pinpoint a mobile speed camera so other drivers can see when using the app. If you want information provided by other drivers, open Google Maps in CarPlay and tap Settings > Alert options > All alerts.

Some navigation apps will send warning alerts without actively navigating, as long as the app is running passively in the background. Radarbot sends alerts for fixed and red light cameras through CarPlay if you have a Gold membership. Roadar adds Flock cameras to the mix, along with other license plate readers mixed in, with speed and red light camera alerts. If you're more concerned about Flock cameras, FlockHopper is free and works with CarPlay as well.

It can, though it depends on what navigation app you're using. With Apple Maps, the Speed Limit toggle is in Settings > Apps > Maps > Driving. The posted limit will appear on screen while you navigate. With the Waze app, make sure you're disconnected from CarPlay, open Waze and tap Settings > Speedometer > Show Speedometer > Set Preferences > Show Speed Limit. Google Maps is similar to Waze, with the speed limit located in the speedometer settings. Open the Google Maps app, tap your profile picture and tap Settings > Navigation > Driving > Speedometer.

Stock CarPlay doesn't include a speedometer, but apps like Waze and Google Maps will display current speeds through CarPlay if you want. Both Google Maps and Waze will warn you if your speeds climb too high, and Waze will give you a heads-up if speed limits are about to drop sharply. In response to car manufacturers ditching CarPlay, Apple introduced CarPlay Ultra, which displays your current speed on the instrument cluster, unlike regular CarPlay. CarPlay Ultra is fully integrated, so it's not an informational speed display, as Google Maps makes clear about its own speedometer.

#223. What pet cemeteries reveal about being human

Editor’s Note:  Eric Tourigny is a lecturer in historical archaeology at Newcastle University, UK. His research interprets osteological and material culture remains alongside historic texts to examine changing human-animal relationships in Europe and North America over the past 500 years. The views expressed in this commentary are his own. Read more opinion on CNN.

Why do we bury our departed loved ones in a cemetery? A primary purpose is to provide survivors with an opportunity to grieve and gain a sense of closure. The cemetery is a place for the living as much as it is a place for the dead.

But what about when the dearly departed are not human – but our pets?

The Spanish city of Barcelona recently announced that it will be investing in the establishment of the country’s first public pet cemetery. Set to open next year, it will offer both burials and cremations – with an estimated 7,000 carried out each year.

For me, as someone who has spent years researching the development of pet cemeteries elsewhere in the world, this news came as a shock. Barcelona is a densely populated city with limited privately owned land – one where 50% of families own a pet.

How did a city that is home to 180,000 dogs not already have a public pet cemetery? Until now, the service was only provided by the private sector, according to Barcelona’s Councilor for Climate Emergency and Ecological Transition, Eloi Badia. He added that the municipal-funded initiative was sparked by “constant public demand.”

After all, public pet cemeteries have been around in Europe and the Americas since the late 19th century. Britain’s first public pet cemetery appeared in London’s Hyde Park in 1881. New York’s Hartsdale pet cemetery was founded in 1896, followed a few years later by Paris’ ornate Cimetière des Chiens in 1899.

I became interested in the history of modern pet burial practices while investigating the archaeological record of a centuries-old house in Toronto. I came across a (very) large dog buried in the back garden which, according to the historical record, was occupied between 1840 and 1870.

This dog survived to an elderly age but, sadly, suffered from degenerative joint disease and severe infections during his last months. His ailments progressed to such a state that suggest he received some level of care in his final weeks. He then was buried in a personal plot behind the family home.

This elderly dog led me to think about the different ways people interact with the bodies of their pets after death. Could this behavior be reflective of the relationships they held with their animals in life? In this instance, why take the time to carefully bury a dog in its own space when other, arguably easier options existed?

This, after all, was an era when people often disposed of their dead pets in the river, or might have sold their bodies for meat and skin.

Good hygiene is an obvious reason to choose a burial – no one wants decomposing animal bodies in the street or their garden – but that wouldn’t immediately warrant a personalized, dedicated burial and gravestone.

The most straight forward option would be to dispose of a deceased animal with the household waste. But such treatment would evidently feel less ceremonious and would not offer appropriate emotional closure to what was likely an important relationship.

Like the burial of people, the burial of pets is an intimate cultural practice, one that changes over time and is reflective of the changing relationships that a society has with its cherished creatures.

My study of historic gravestones and epitaphs in Britain from the Victorian period to today shows this changing human-animal relationship. In the 19th century, gravestones were often dedicated to a “loving friend” or “devoted companion,” suggesting pets were mostly considered important friends.

By the early 20th century, pets had become members of the family – evidenced by the appearance of family surnames on the gravestones, and loving epitaphs written by “Mummy and Daddy.”

By the early 20th century, pets had become members of the family – evidenced by the appearance of family surnames on the gravestones, and loving epitaphs written by “Mummy and Daddy.”

Society’s changing attitude towards the role of animals in the afterlife can also be found. Fast-forward a few decades later, and gravestones were more likely to reference a reunion then earlier ones. For example, the owners of Denny, the “brave little cat” buried in an east London cemetery in 1952, wrote on his epitaph “God bless until we meet again.”

I wonder what the epitaphs in Barcelona’s new cemetery will reveal about modern Catalan relationships with animals.

Over time, our ways of treating our animal dead appear to reflect an even closer relationship in life. Once strictly forbidden by law, the last decade saw many jurisdictions, like the state of New York, allowing the co-burial of cremated animals and people, which will undoubtedly lead to changing funerary and commemoration practices for both humans and animals.

For me, the most remarkable similarity between modern and historic pet cemeteries is the striking evidence for the heartbreak and taboos around grieving for animals.

The connection that someone has with their pet can be just as strong and just as significant as their relationships with other humans. Yet today, as in over 100 years ago, individuals continue to struggle to find the appropriate outlet to express their pain, hiding heartache for fear of the social repercussions that might come with public acknowledgment of the existence of such a bond.

The RSPCA reassures the public on its website that they should not feel shame for their grief. In the UK, charities like the Blue Cross and Rainbow Bridge Pet Loss Grief Center offer counseling to bereaved humans.

Close relationships between people and animals have existed for millennia, but in western European cultures, there were few acceptable ways to mourn that relationship. As society becomes more accepting of the importance of human-animal relationships to our collective wellbeing, it is not surprising to see us follow rituals resembling those we use to mourn the loss of our closest human relationships.

At an estimated cost of €200 ($217) per service at the new Barcelona cemetery, it is important to acknowledge that this opportunity to grieve will not be financially available to everyone in the city.

This will not be a space for all of the city’s pets. Pet owners may opt to keep cremated remains within their home or spread out ashes in a meaningful location instead. Online forums and digital pet cemeteries also provide other opportunities to commemorate the relationship and express grief.

Whether one chooses a pet cemetery or not, there are many acceptable ways to express your grief – and to remember your relationship with the important animals in your life.

#222. How one 13-year-old is helping solve a huge solar panel limitation

Tired of moving solar-powered Christmas lights, a seventh grader built a tracker that lets gravity do the work.

Jason Chang was sick of his mother asking him to adjust the family's solar-powered Christmas lights to get more sun, so he devised a solution with big potential. The 13-year-old seventh grader at Worcester Academy in Massachusetts created a solar tracker that utilizes water and gravity to move a solar panel without the need for a motor, a sunlight sensor or electricity to power the mechanism.

The prototype was less than $25 and generated about 20 percent more voltage than a stationary panel in outdoor tests, CBS Boston reports. The contraption tackles a basic limitation of fixed solar panels: the inability to change position as the sun moves across the sky. This teenager's bright idea is attracting national attention. Here's how it works.

Chang's invention is similar to a seesaw. A small solar panel is mounted on a rotating wooden structure, with water dripping into a bucket on one side. The frame tilts the panel throughout the day as the bucket fills, increasing its weight. There's no sensor needed to determine the sun's position, and the drip rate is adjusted to keep the panel tilting at approximately the correct speed.

It's not difficult to get the process started. Simply pull the plug to set the water in motion. However, it took a lot more work to get that flow just right. Chang spent over a year refining the project, jotting down his tests in a notebook and using recycled materials for much of the construction. And while gravity is free of cost, trying to make it work on a schedule takes a little engineering.

The reported 20 percent improvement also needs to be examined. In the outdoor comparisons, Chang's setup was able to generate higher voltage, but that doesn't necessarily translate to a 20 percent increase in power or total energy output. To calculate those gains, current readings and energy measurements over time would be required, but were not included in the report. It's a positive outcome for a student prototype, but not a guarantee to save you 20 percent on your electric bill.

Using water and gravity to follow the sun isn't entirely new. There are commercial trackers on the market that can move with the sun, but they cost more than fixed units. There are also some build-it-yourself designs similar to Chang's concept. Engineering for Change promotes a SunSaluter rotating solar panel kit with a suggested retail price of $50. That cost doesn't include the panel, battery, and other components. Chang's version offers another inexpensive DIY take on the idea, rather than a commercially ready replacement for existing trackers.

There's a practical reason why most rooftop solar panels aren't designed to move around. Trackers can boost energy yields from ground-mounted arrays, but they also add costs and maintenance. It's easy to tilt a small wooden frame, but mounting moving panels on a roof where they have to withstand wind and rain is where it gets complicated. Any extra electricity would have to be worth the investment and maintenance. Another fixed panel might be a lot less hassle for some homeowners.

Sure, motor-free tracking could still appeal to people running small off-grid systems, where every bit of power counts. However, water has its own set of issues. While cold weather can actually boost solar panel efficiency, a mechanism that relies on flowing water has an unwelcome winter issue: ice, which is why Chang is working on a winter version.

CBS did not say how often the water needs to be refilled, how often the tracker needs to be reset, or whether the design has been tested with full-size panels in strong winds. Regardless, Chang's work as a seventh-grader is exceptional. In 2026, he was one of 55 students recognized as National STEM Champions.

#218. How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause

COVID-19 lockdowns cut global fire activity by 12.3 percent.

Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people’s lives. A series of massive bushfires from 2019 to 2020 swept across southeastern Australia and destroyed thousands of homes. Recently, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires spread widely across the city, resulting in massive damage to local communities.

Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts. Measuring people’s impact on fire is difficult because of the mix of human and natural influences.

A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity.

Fire doesn’t just happen anywhere. Although plenty of flammable materials exist in natural settings, not every place experiences wildfires. Some prairies burn almost every year, while many forests go without big fires for hundreds of years. Researchers explain these differences in terms of fire regimes, which are patterns describing when, how often, and how widely and intensely fires occur.

Weather is a major factor affecting fire regimes. An abundance of rain helps grow grass and trees that can become fuel for fires. Whether they do or not, however, can depend on the moisture inside plants; plants with enough moisture do not burn easily. By contrast, dry conditions make them more likely to catch fire. When a drought lasts, vegetation becomes increasingly flammable. Strong winds also accelerate fire growth and spread enormously.

Human activity often combines with weather conditions to cause fires. Even routine outdoor recreation can accidentally start a fire. More people venture outdoors during sunny, drier times of the year, increasing the risk of accidental fires when dry vegetation is more likely to be present.

The double-sided role of humans in fire also adds to the difficulty. Humans do start fires, but they also put them out. Firefighters contain fires that could have gone worse if no action had been taken and can keep them from spreading. Humans can also take preventative actions, such as clearing flammable material.

Sometimes the line between starting fires and preventing them becomes blurred. One way to clear out flammable material is to intentionally set fires to make future fires more manageable. However, these fires are hard to distinguish from other fires through satellite monitoring.

An experiment is one way to find out how humans affect wildfires. If everyone stayed home under the same weather, their impact on fires would be revealed. This is why Wang’s research team focused on the COVID-19 era. It was what’s called a “natural experiment,” in which experimental conditions arose without any action by researchers.

Wang explained: “Human activity and climate normally vary together, because seasons, farming calendars, and weather all shape both fire and human behavior. The early-2020 lockdowns produced an abrupt, large-scale drop in human mobility, and the timing differed across countries while the weather did not change in the same way. This gave us a natural experiment.”

The researchers defined the period of restricted mobility by checking regional lockdown orders and mobile phone location data. Data from NASA and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Suomi NPP satellite helped the team track fires. Its VIIRS sensor detects heat signatures from fires at a spatial resolution of 375 meters. Each hot spot the satellite detects counts as an active-fire detection, meaning one large fire can appear as multiple spots. However, the satellite records both wildfires and prescribed burns without distinguishing between them. As a result, the intent behind each fire remains unknown.

In the study, detections during the 2020 restriction periods were compared with those from the same weeks in 2013–2019. Weather conditions weren’t exactly the same as in past years, which was accounted for.

The results show that areas under lockdown in the first half of 2020 had about 12.3 percent fewer active-fire detections than the recent-past average. The drop varied by vegetation type. In forests, fires decreased by about 27.7 percent, while grasslands decreased by 8.4 percent. Shrublands, savannas, and croplands didn’t show much difference. The researchers interpret this to mean that humans are a major cause of fires in forests and grasslands.

Controlling for weather factors was important in the study. Without adjustments, the drop was only 5.8 percent, which was not statistically significant. After controlling for weather, however, the estimated decline increased to 12.3 percent. If weather in 2020 were more favorable to fires than in previous years, it might have masked some of the human impact.

The 12.3 percent decrease in fire detections doesn’t mean that humans directly caused this share of fires. Restricting human activity shrank both humans’ impact on starting fires and likely limited their impact on extinguishing them. The 12.3 percent figure is the net effect after these two opposing forces partly cancel out.

Wang said, “The 12.3 percent is a net effect, not the share of fires caused by humans; opposing changes in ignition and suppression mean it does not capture the full magnitude of human influence.”

In regional data, some areas experienced a considerable increase in fire after human mobility was restricted. Most of South America, southern Africa, and northeast Asia saw an increase in fire during the COVID-19 lockdowns. Notable increases include 31.4 percent in Colombia, 25.4 percent in India, and 70.7 percent in Honduras.

There are no direct field data showing why this occurred. The researchers inferred that diminished fire suppression capacity resulted in more fires in these locations, but Wang acknowledged, “It is an inference, not a direct observation.” That inference was based in part on earlier studies that suggested that weaker fire management in Colombia and Madagascar contributed to increased fires.

One line of evidence is how fires reacted to different levels of mobility loss, based on fire counts in 0.5-degree grid cells. In countries with fewer fires, fire declined in almost a straight line as mobility decreased. But countries that experienced more fires showed a slow increase that leveled off at about 27 percent on average as mobility fell. The researchers interpreted this as a sign that different mechanisms were at work. The steady decline fits fewer human-driven ignitions, while the gradual rise points to weakened suppression. But Wang mentioned that there could be other reasons, such as changes in local land use.

Mobility restrictions may also have disrupted fire management activities, which could mean that fewer fires were set for management purposes. The researchers examined 12 countries with records of prescribed burning. The area burned by prescribed fires in 2020 decreased by about half compared to the 2013–2019 average. Of course, the locations and sizes of prescribed burns also shift from year to year with fire return intervals and land-management cycles, which complicates this analysis.

When areas subjected to prescribed burning were excluded in those 12 countries, the decline in fires there shrank from 45.3 percent to 27.8 percent.

This research has limits partly because it relied on mobile phone data to track human movement. This kind of data might not capture human activity in rural areas where coverage may be limited. Also, the analysis focused only on the first half of each year, so the impact on regions where fires happen more frequently in the latter half of the year, such as the western US, may not have been fully captured.

Wang explained that this quasi-experimental design provides strong associational evidence but is not a controlled experiment.

Wang emphasized that the study is not an evaluation of fire policies. The analysis does, however, suggest that there’s no single ideal policy response. Where fires decreased, human ignition seems to dominate. In those areas, reducing accidental ignitions through public education and maintaining beneficial prescribed burning can be important. On the other hand, areas where fires increased might need to address reduced monitoring and suppression. Maintaining firefighting and patrol capacity during disruptions can be important there.

Wang added, “Overall, a uniform policy is unlikely to work, and strategies should be tailored to local human-fire relationships.” Fire-risk projections might benefit from accounting for human behavior. That way, more accurate fire projections can be made even as weather and society change.

Cell Reports Sustainability, 2026. DOI: 10.1016/j.crsus.2026.100860
